title: Carrying Burdens and Boasting in the Cross
summary: Paul gives practical instructions for life in the Spirit: restore those who fall with gentleness, carry one another's burdens, support those who teach, and keep sowing what is good without growing weary. Then, writing the closing lines in his own hand, he exposes the motives of those pressing circumcision and declares that he will boast only in the cross of Christ, because what counts is a new creation.
story: Chapter 5 set the life of the Spirit against the works of the flesh. Chapter 6 shows what that life looks like inside a real congregation, where people sin, carry heavy loads, teach and learn, and are tempted to compare themselves with one another. Then Paul takes the pen and gathers up the whole letter in a few lines. The dispute over circumcision, which began in chapter 1 with a warning against a different gospel, ends with a declaration that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision matters, only a new creation. The letter closes as it began, with grace, and without the warm personal greetings that end most of Paul's letters, a sign of how serious the situation was.
historical:
Ancient letters were usually written down by a trained scribe, and the sender might add a closing line in his own hand as a mark of authenticity and personal attention. Paul did this in several letters (1 Corinthians 16:21; Colossians 4:18; 2 Thessalonians 3:17), and Romans 16:22 names the scribe who wrote that letter, Tertius. In Galatians 6:11 Paul draws attention to the large letters of his own handwriting. Whether this means he wrote the whole letter himself or only the closing section is debated; most scholars think he took over from a scribe at this point. Why the letters were large is unknown. Suggestions include poor eyesight (connected by some with 4:13-15), hands damaged by manual labor or beatings, or simply emphasis, like writing in bold.

The marks of Jesus that Paul bears on his body (v. 17) most likely refer to scars from his sufferings as an apostle. He was stoned and left for dead at Lystra, one of the cities in the southern part of the Roman province of Galatia (Acts 14:19), and he lists beatings, lashings, and a stoning in 2 Corinthians 11:24-25. If some of the Galatian churches were in that region, they may have seen those wounds for themselves.
cultural:
The word for marks (stigmata) was used for brands or tattoos placed on slaves to show ownership, on soldiers in some settings, and on devotees of certain gods. Paul's scars show whose he is. Against the agitators' demand for the mark of circumcision, he points to the marks of suffering for Christ.

Sowing and reaping (vv. 7-9) drew on the farming life nearly every reader knew. A farmer who planted one crop could not expect to harvest another, and the harvest came only after long patience. Support for teachers (v. 6) reflects the practice of sharing material goods with those who gave instruction in the faith, a pattern Paul defends elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:14), though he often supported himself by his own work. The family of faith (v. 10) uses household language: believers are kin, and ancient households were expected to provide first for their own members, while Paul extends doing good to everyone.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 10 are a series of short, proverb-like instructions, some of which seem to pull against each other on purpose. Carry one another's burdens (v. 2) sits beside each one should carry his own load (v. 5); the Greek uses two different words, the first for a crushing weight, the second for the ordinary pack a person carries, so Paul is calling both for mutual help and for personal responsibility. Verses 11 to 18 are the letter's closing, written in Paul's own hand, and they work as a summary of the whole argument: the motives of the agitators, the centrality of the cross, the irrelevance of circumcision, and a blessing on those who walk by this rule. The contrast between boasting in the flesh (v. 13) and boasting in the cross (v. 14) is the chapter's hinge.

outline.t: Restoring the fallen and carrying burdens
Sowing and reaping; doing good to all
Paul's own hand: boasting only in the cross, a new creation
The marks of Jesus and a final blessing

doctrines.note: The church is a family of faith in which members restore those who fall, carry one another's burdens, share with their teachers, and do good. Life in the Spirit is life together.
The cross is the only ground of Paul's boasting (v. 14). Through it the world, with its systems of status and achievement, has been crucified to him, and he to it.
God is not mocked: what a person sows, he reaps (v. 7). Grace does not cancel moral consequence. Sowing to the flesh ends in destruction, and sowing to the Spirit in eternal life.
What counts is a new creation (v. 15). Paul sees in Christ the beginning of God's renewal of the world, already at work in those who belong to him.

words.note: Baros, burden or heavy weight. In verse 2 it describes loads too heavy for one person, such as temptation, grief, or hardship. Carrying them together fulfills the law of Christ, a phrase most readers connect with Jesus's command to love one another and with the self-giving pattern of his own life.

Phortion, load or pack, the ordinary burden a soldier or traveler carries. Jesus uses it for his light burden in Matthew 11:30. In verse 5 it refers to each person's own responsibility before God, which no one else can carry for them.

Ktisis, creation. Paul speaks of a new creation (v. 15; compare 2 Corinthians 5:17), echoing the prophets' hope of new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17). In Christ, God has begun to make the world new, and that, not ethnic or religious marks, is what finally counts.

Stigma, mark or brand. It was used for marks of ownership burned or cut into the skin. Paul's scars from suffering for Christ mark him as Christ's servant, in contrast to the mark of circumcision the agitators were demanding.

christ: The chapter brings the whole letter to rest on the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. The cross is Paul's only boast because it is God's act of salvation, not a human achievement, and through it the old world of rank, merit, and religious status loses its hold. Christ's own way of life stands behind the call to carry one another's burdens, since he carried ours; the law of Christ is love shaped by his self-giving. Through him a new creation has begun (v. 15). Paul's own body, marked by suffering for Jesus, shows what it looks like to belong to a crucified Lord.

hard.q: Who is “the Israel of God” in verse 16?
hard.a:
The phrase appears nowhere else in the Bible, and its meaning is debated. Many interpreters read it as the whole church, Jewish and Gentile believers together, whom Paul has just described as Abraham's seed (3:29) and children of promise (4:28); on this reading the word translated even joins the two phrases, so that those who walk by this rule are the Israel of God. Others argue that Paul never elsewhere calls the church Israel, and that the Greek word most often means and; on their reading Paul pronounces peace on believers generally and then adds a blessing on Jewish believers in particular, or on the Jewish people whom God will yet show mercy to, as in Romans 11:26. Translations vary accordingly.

The question matters because it touches how Christians understand the relationship between the church and Israel, a subject on which faithful traditions differ. Whatever the phrase means, Paul's point is that belonging to God's people comes through Christ and the new creation, not through circumcision.

questions: Paul asks the spiritually mature to restore those who fall with gentleness and to watch themselves. What makes that kind of restoration hard to do well?
How do you tell the difference between a burden you should share with others and a load you are responsible to carry yourself?
Paul says he boasts only in the cross. What do people you know, including you, tend to boast in instead?
